A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ATC research work. Their main sections, Figures 1–11, equations, and Appendices A.1–A.7 are readable and can be matched reliably despite reflow and revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic simulations and NAB CPU-usage experiments, including regret curves, Monte Carlo estimates, and sensitivity analyses in Section 5 and Appendix A.1.

after.justification: v2 retains the original synthetic and NAB experiments, including the empirical results in Figures 3–9 and Appendix A.1.

M1.justification: Scalar ATC in Algorithm 1, its restart rule, running-mean predictions, and multiscale approximation remain unchanged. Appendix A.7 revises the vector extension's detection threshold by introducing a universal multiplicative constant C0: compare v1 Equation (93) with v2 Equation (89). This is a limited threshold-calibration revision.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Gaussian piecewise-stationary synthetic environments and NAB AWS CPU-usage series, including dense changes and adversarial scenarios. The additional discussion of exponential-family, regression, and dependent-observation settings proposes future extensions rather than reporting new evaluations.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain sliding-window and discounted-mean baselines, the same constant-threshold detectors, and the efficient ATC variant. Newly cited related methods are not added as evaluated comparators. The passive baselines' observation-timing revision is an evaluation-protocol change.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1.1 changes the sliding-window and discounted-mean formulas from including observations through t to using observations through t−1. This revises the reported prediction-time information available to those baselines. The sliding-window denominator and lower summation limit remain unchanged, leaving an indexing inconsistency. The PDFs do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The dense-change, passive-baseline, constant-threshold, variance-misspecification, adversarial-environment, and change-count analyses were already present in v1 Appendix A.1. v2 adds a main-text overview of these retained analyses without adding tests or case studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report 5000 Monte Carlo replications for Figure 3(c), 1000 runs for the supplementary simulations, and the same stated 95% confidence-interval procedure using ±1.96 standard errors. No new empirical uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing practice appears.

E6.justification: The plotted empirical results in Figures 3–9 are identical, including the comparator curves and regret trends. The accompanying findings remain unchanged. Revised baseline formulas do not establish new results or a performance improvement under comparable settings.

T1.justification: Several central formal statements are corrected. Section 2 starts regret at t=2 and changes the environment class to at most S changes. Lemma 3.1 becomes a high-probability, no-alarm implication for deterministic restart indices, drops the additive M² term, and receives a reorganized proof in Appendix A.6. Theorem 4.2 explicitly requires M≥c0σ and S<T and removes the log-log qualification. Further revisions address upper-bound constants, proof boundary cases, and vector concentration scaling. These materially revise the guarantees while retaining their leading regret rates.

C1.justification: The central contributions—selective detection, control of endogenous confounding, and nearly minimax-optimal anytime tracking—remain intact. Section 1.2 removes the lower-order log-log qualification from its stated lower-bound contribution, giving a limited strengthening of that claim.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad claim that faster or slower threshold growth precludes optimal guarantees with a qualified explanation of controlled contamination and recovery. Section 4.3 softens the inference from the lower bound to sublinear-regret achievability. The conclusion adds substantive discussion of extension requirements, online variance calibration, dependent observations, and gradual drift.

D1.justification: Section 5 replaces v1's promise of future code availability with a statement of public availability and an explicit implementation repository link. This adds actionable access information; the repository's contents were not inspected. Most data-processing instructions and experimental hyperparameters are retained.

R1.justification: Section 1.3 adds positioning relative to gradual non-stationarity and window selection, window-limited CUSUM, and joint detection-and-estimation, citing Huang and Wang, Xie and colleagues, Moustakides and colleagues, and Chen and colleagues. The bandit discussion is refined, including replacing Auer et al. (2019) with Cao et al. (2019), without redefining the paper's overall research position.

P1.justification: v2 expands selected background, related-work, proof-explanation, and future-work passages; reorganizes Appendix A.6; and makes grammatical corrections. It retitles the conclusion and removes the generic Impact Statement. The main section sequence and appendix organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: All eleven figures retain their graphical content and panel structures. Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 shift relative to surrounding discussion, and other material reflows. Figure 6's caption changes from saying curves coincide to describing them as visually indistinguishable. No figures or tables are newly added.

improvement.justification: v2 better aligns the formal statements with the existing analysis: regret begins at t=2, the SNR guarantee states its confidence and no-alarm conditions, and the lower bound exposes its non-degeneracy requirement. Clearer positioning and implementation access also help readers verify and use the work. These are useful improvements to the existing contribution, tempered by the incomplete sliding-window formula correction and the absence of evidence that the revised baseline protocol was reflected in the unchanged plots.
